title: PivotTables: the basics
goal: Insert a PivotTable with the keyboard, drag fields into Rows, Columns, Values and Filters, predict what it will show, and refresh it with Alt + F5 when the data changes.

steps.text:
Your manager asks: “How much did each region sell?”

Here are just 7 orders, but **imagine 5,000**. Writing a formula per region is slow, and one new region means more work.

A **PivotTable** is a summary table Excel builds for you when you **drag** column headings into boxes. No formulas to type. The table on the right is what one would show: regions down the side, total sales beside each.

In real Excel the pivot usually opens on a **new sheet**. Here it sits beside the data so you can see both.

steps.prompt:
A pivot needs a **clean list**: one heading on every column, no blank rows or columns inside, and one kind of thing per column. Yours is.

Click any cell in the list, then tap [[Alt]], [[N]], [[V]] one after another: **Insert → PivotTable**. In the menu that opens you'd pick **From Table/Range**; Excel guesses the whole list for you. On a Mac, use the **Insert** tab → **PivotTable**.
clues: Press and release Alt, then N, then V.

steps.prompt: Before inserting a pivot you check the list on the left. What do you fix first?
options: Sort Region from A to Z
Name column C and delete the blank row
Add a Total row at the bottom
steps.explain: A blank heading stops Excel building the pivot, and a blank row cuts the list short, so only the rows above it get summarised. Fix both and Excel picks up the full list.
wrongFeedback: A pivot groups the regions by itself, so sorting the source changes nothing.
A Total row would be read as one more order, so every figure would be counted **twice**. Never type totals inside pivot data.
clues: Which of these would make Excel stop reading the list?

steps.prompt:
The field list has four boxes: **Filters**, **Columns**, **Rows** and **Values**.

Your manager wants “one line per region, with its sales added up beside it”. What do you drag where?
options: Region to Values, Sales to Rows
Region to Filters, Sales to Columns
Region to Rows, Sales to Values
steps.explain: **Rows** gives one line for each different Region, and **Values** is the number Excel adds up. That is the table you saw in the first step.
wrongFeedback: Values is the box for the numbers to add up. Putting Region there would count the words instead.
Filters only hides things, and Columns would spread Sales across the top. Neither gives one line per region.
clues: The box that makes one line per item is Rows; the box that holds numbers to add is Values.

steps.prompt:
You dragged **Region** to Rows and **Sales** to Values. The pivot sits in `E1:F5`, with South left blank.

What will the pivot show for South? Work it out from the list with a **SUMIFS** in ==F4==: add Sales where Region matches the label in `E4`.
steps.explain: **2430.** That's 1200 + 750 + 480, the three South orders. A pivot is SUMIFS done for you, once per row label, even when there are 5,000 rows.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Start with `=` so Excel knows it's a formula.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket and comma.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use `SUMIFS` to add Sales for one region.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: South has three orders (1200, 750, 480). Sum Sales `C2:C8` where Region `A2:A8` equals `E4`.

clues: `=SUMIFS(sum range, criteria range, criteria)`: the Sales column first.
The criteria is the label in `E4`.

steps.prompt:
Now drag **Product** to **Columns** as well. Products run across the top, regions down the side, and each cell shows the sales for one pair.

What will the cell where **South** meets **Coffee** show? Put your **SUMIFS** in ==F4==. It needs two conditions.
steps.explain: **1680.** South's two Coffee orders, 1200 and 480. Using only the region would give 2430, and only the product 2700; the cell needs both conditions.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Start with `=` so Excel knows it's a formula.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket and comma.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use `SUMIFS` with two pairs of range and criteria.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Both must match: Region `A2:A8` equals `E4` **and** Product `B2:B8` equals `F1`.

clues: Add a second pair to the formula: product range, then the label in `F1`.

steps.prompt:
Drag **Product** to **Filters** and pick **Tea** from the little menu above the pivot. Now the whole pivot shows Tea orders only.

What will **Grand Total** show in ==F7==? Work it out from the list with a **SUMIFS**, not by adding the cells above it.
steps.explain: **2250.** Tea orders only: 500 + 750 + 1000. The Filters box doesn't add a row or column; it just decides which orders the pivot is allowed to count.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Start with `=` so Excel knows it's a formula.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket and comma.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use `SUMIFS` to add Sales where Product is Tea.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Only Tea orders count: Product `B2:B8` equals `F1`. All sales together would be 4950.

clues: One condition this time: Product equals the word in `F1`.

steps.prompt:
Mira drags **Product** into Values instead of Sales. Product is a column of **words**, and Excel can't add words, so it quietly switches to **Count**. The heading changes to “Count of Product”.

What will the pivot show for South? Use **COUNTIF** in ==F4==.
steps.explain: **3.** South has three orders, so Excel counts 3 and shows no rupees at all. Always read the heading: “Sum of Sales” is money, “Count of Product” is just how many rows.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Start with `=` so Excel knows it's a formula.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket and comma.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use `COUNTIF` to count the South rows.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Count the rows where Region `A2:A8` equals `E4`. Adding Sales would give 2430, but this pivot counts words.

clues: `=COUNTIF(range, criteria)`: how many cells in Region match `E4`?

steps.prompt: Another pivot shows “**Count of Sales**” even though Sales is a column of numbers. What's the most likely cause?
options: Some Sales cells are text or blank
Region is in the Rows box
steps.explain: Excel looks at the column when you drop it in Values: if even some cells are text (like “n/a”) or blank, it defaults to **Count**. Clean the source cells, or switch the value to Sum in **Value Field Settings**.
wrongFeedback: A stale pivot shows old numbers, but it would still say “Sum of”.
Rows only decides the lines. The Sum or Count choice depends on what the Sales column holds.
clues: Look at the Sales column for anything that isn't a number.

steps.prompt:
You fix an order: South's Coffee sale in `C3` was 1200, but it should be **1500**. You type it in and look at the pivot on screen.

What does South show now?
steps.explain: A pivot is a **snapshot**. It does not follow the source live, so it still says 2430 until you refresh it. This catches out everyone once.
wrongFeedback: It will be 2730 after a refresh, but not before. Unlike a formula, a pivot doesn't recalculate on its own.
Nothing is broken. The pivot simply hasn't looked at the new number yet.
clues: Is a pivot live like `=SUM()`, or a snapshot?

steps.prompt:
Click inside the pivot (`F4` is) and press [[Alt]] + [[F5]]: **Refresh**. South jumps to 2730 and the Grand Total follows.

To refresh every pivot in the file, use [[Ctrl]] + [[Alt]] + [[F5]]. On a Mac, use **Data → Refresh All**.

Last one, from memory.

A delivery team's pivot has **City** in Rows, **Day** in Filters set to **Sat**, and **Orders** in Values. What number will it show for **Pune**? Put the answer in ==G5==.
steps.explain: **23.** Pune's two Saturday orders, 15 + 8. Pune on any day is 40, and every Saturday is 43, so both the Rows label and the Filter had to count.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Start with `=` so Excel knows it's a formula.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket and comma.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The pivot counts only Pune **and** only Saturday. Pune's Saturday orders are 15 and 8.

clues: Rows decides which city; Filters decides which day. Both are conditions.
Sum of Orders: add the Orders column `D2:D8`.
